Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that despite President Bush's low approval ratings, people will soon "start to thank this president for what he's done." Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says "there is no greater honor than to serve this country," "So we can sit here and talk about the long record, but what I would say to you is that this president has faced tougher circumstances than perhaps at any time since the end of World War II, and he has delivered policies that are going to stand the test of time," Rice said in an interview that aired on CBS' "Sunday Morning." The secretary of state brushed off reports that suggest the United States' image is suffering abroad.  She praised the administration's ability to change the conversation in the Middle East. "This isn't a popularity contest. I'm sorry, it isn't. What the administration is responsible to do is to make good choices about Americans' interests and values in the long run -- not for today's headlines, but for history's judgment," she said. "And I am quite certain that when the final chapters are written and it's clear that Saddam Hussein's Iraq is gone in favor of an Iraq that is favorable to the future of the Middle East; when the history is written of a U.S.-China relationship that is better than it's ever been; an India relationship that is deeper and better than it's ever been; a relationship with Brazil and other countries of the left of Latin America, better than it's ever been ... "When one looks at what we've been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I'll wait for history's judgment and not today's headlines." Asked by CBS' Rita Braver why some former diplomats say Americans are disliked around the world, Rice said that's "just not true." "I know what U.S. policy has achieved. And so I don't know what diplomats you're talking to, but look at the record," she said. Rice said she wasn't bothered by criticism about her or the administration's polices, saying if a person in her business is not being criticized, "you're not doing something right." "I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes, I -- there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time," she said. Asked about historians who say Bush is one of the worst presidents, Rice said those "aren't very good historians." "If you're making historical judgments before an administration is already out -- even out of office, and if you're trying to make historical judgments when the nature of the Middle East is still to be determined, and when one cannot yet judge the effects of decisions that this President has taken on what the Middle East will become -- I mean, for goodness' sakes, good historians are still writing books about George Washington. Good historians are certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she said. Rice, 54, said she has enjoyed working in the Bush administration during the last eight years, first as national security adviser, then as secretary of state. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she said, adding that there is also no greater challenge. Rice said when the new administration takes over, she plans to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University and write two books -- one on foreign policy and one about her parents.

# Rice Defends Bush Legacy in "Sunday Morning" Interview

Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice offered a spirited defense of President George W. Bush's legacy during an appearance on CBS "Sunday Morning," pushing back against critics who have questioned the administration's foreign policy decisions and handling of key domestic challenges.

Rice, who served as Bush's national security adviser during his first term before becoming the nation's top diplomat, argued that history would ultimately view the former president more favorably than contemporary assessments have allowed.

## A Measured Assessment

"I think when the passions of the moment cool, people will look back and see a president who made difficult decisions in extraordinarily difficult times," Rice said during the interview. She emphasized that leaders often face judgments that shift considerably as time provides greater perspective.

Rice pointed to the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as a defining moment that shaped much of the administration's agenda, noting that the president faced circumstances few of his predecessors had encountered.

## Addressing the Critics

When pressed on some of the administration's most controversial decisions, including the war in Iraq, Rice acknowledged that not everything unfolded as planned but defended the fundamental intentions behind the policies.

"Were there mistakes made? Of course. Show me an administration where there weren't," she said. "But the desire to protect the American people and to spread the values of freedom and democracy—that was always at the heart of what we did."

Rice also highlighted what she considered underappreciated accomplishments, including the administration's efforts to combat HIV/AIDS in Africa through the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, which she described as saving millions of lives.

## Reflections on Leadership

Throughout the conversation, Rice reflected on her personal relationship with the former president, describing him as thoughtful and deeply committed to his responsibilities. She characterized the decision-making process within the administration as more deliberative than critics often portrayed.

The former secretary of state, who currently serves in academia, has largely maintained a lower public profile in recent years but occasionally speaks out on matters of foreign policy and national governance.

## Looking Forward

Rice concluded the interview by expressing confidence that the passage of time would bring a more balanced evaluation of the Bush years, urging Americans to consider the full context in which decisions were made.

The interview adds to an ongoing national conversation about presidential legacies and how history ultimately renders its verdict on those who have occupied the Oval Office.

---

# Rice Reflects on Legacy, Looks Ahead as Administration Winds Down

**WASHINGTON** — Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice offered a spirited defense of the Bush administration's foreign policy record this week, acknowledging criticism while outlining her vision for America's diplomatic future and hinting at her own plans once she leaves office.

Speaking to reporters at the State Department, Rice pointed to what she characterized as significant achievements during her tenure, particularly on the African continent and in the realm of global health initiatives.

"When you look at what we've accomplished on issues like combating HIV/AIDS through PEPFAR, or our engagement with emerging democracies, I believe history will judge these efforts favorably," Rice said, referencing the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, which dramatically expanded treatment access across sub-Saharan Africa.

## Addressing the Critics

Rice did not shy away from the substantial criticism that has marked much of the administration's foreign policy, particularly regarding the Iraq War and America's standing among traditional allies.

"No one can look at a landscape as complex as the one we've navigated and claim everything was done perfectly," she conceded. "But the decisions we made were made in good faith, in the interest of American security and, we believed, in service of a freer world."

Critics have long faulted Rice and the administration for the intelligence failures preceding the Iraq invasion, the handling of the war's aftermath, and strained relationships with European partners. When pressed on these points, Rice emphasized that the challenges facing the incoming administration would benefit from institutional groundwork already laid.

She highlighted diplomatic efforts in the final year of the administration, including engagement on Middle East peace and negotiations concerning North Korea's nuclear program.

## Looking Beyond Washington

As the administration prepares for transition, Rice addressed questions about her own future, signaling a return to academic life rather than a continued role in public office.

"I've always considered myself, first and foremost, an educator," said Rice, who served as provost at Stanford University before entering government service. "I look forward to returning to the classroom, to students, and to writing."

Rice indicated she intends to reflect on her experiences through writing and possibly return to Stanford, where she held a faculty position in political science. She declined to speculate on any future return to public life, saying only that she planned to remain engaged in policy discussions from outside government.

"There's important work to be done in thinking about America's role in the world, and I hope to contribute to that conversation," she said.

## A Complicated Legacy

Political analysts remain divided over how Rice's tenure will ultimately be assessed. Supporters credit her with bringing a more diplomatic tone to the administration's second term and pursuing engagement over confrontation on several fronts. Detractors argue that early decisions cast a long shadow that later diplomacy could not fully overcome.

As one of the most prominent figures of the Bush era and the second woman and second African American to hold the position of Secretary of State, Rice's place in history remains a subject of ongoing debate—one she appears prepared to help shape through her own account in the years ahead.

"I leave this office with a clear conscience and enormous gratitude for the opportunity to serve," Rice said. "The work of diplomacy never ends, and I have every confidence in those who will carry it forward."

---

# Rice Reflects on Bush Administration's Foreign Policy Legacy

**By CNN Staff**

WASHINGTON — Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice offered a candid assessment of how history might judge the Bush administration's foreign policy record, expressing confidence that key decisions across the Middle East, Asia, and Latin America would ultimately be vindicated by time, even as she acknowledged that some judgments remain premature.

## The Middle East: A Long View

Rice defended the administration's approach to the Middle East, arguing that the region's transformation would be measured in decades rather than years. She maintained that the decision to remove Saddam Hussein and the subsequent effort to plant democratic institutions in Iraq represented a fundamental strategic bet on the region's future.

"You cannot judge these things in the moment," Rice suggested in her characteristic measured tone. She argued that the promotion of democratic governance and human freedom, however difficult its implementation, positioned the United States on the right side of history's arc.

Critics have long pointed to the enormous costs of the Iraq war—in lives, resources, and regional stability—and Rice acknowledged that the price was steep. However, she emphasized that establishing a functioning democracy in the heart of the Arab world could eventually reshape expectations across the region.

## China: Managing a Rising Power

On China, Rice expressed cautious optimism about the administration's efforts to integrate Beijing into the international system while managing the complexities of a rising power. She characterized the relationship as one of the most consequential the United States would navigate in the 21st century.

The administration pursued a strategy of engagement combined with hedging—encouraging China to become a "responsible stakeholder" in global affairs while maintaining strong regional alliances. Rice suggested that history would credit the administration with keeping the relationship stable during a period of dramatic Chinese economic growth.

## India: A Landmark Partnership

Perhaps nowhere was Rice more confident about the administration's legacy than on India. The historic civil nuclear agreement between Washington and New Delhi represented what she and others viewed as a signature achievement—a fundamental realignment that transformed a once-distant relationship into a strategic partnership.

Rice argued that recognizing India as a natural democratic partner, and bringing it into the nuclear mainstream despite its non-signatory status to the Non-Proliferation Treaty, would be remembered as a farsighted decision that reshaped the geopolitics of Asia for a generation.

## Latin America: A Mixed Picture

On Latin America, the assessment grew more complicated. Rice acknowledged the challenges of an era marked by the rise of leftist populism, particularly the confrontational posture of leaders like Venezuela's Hugo Chávez.

Still, she pointed to free trade agreements and efforts to strengthen democratic institutions and economic ties with partners across the hemisphere as evidence of constructive engagement. Critics contend the region received insufficient attention amid the administration's focus on the Middle East and the broader war on terror.

## History's Verdict

Throughout her reflections, Rice returned to a consistent theme: that the true measure of foreign policy decisions often becomes clear only with the passage of time. She cited the example of post-World War II statesmen whose choices were criticized in their moment but later celebrated as foundational to decades of stability.

"History has a long arc," Rice has often argued, expressing faith that the administration's emphasis on freedom, democracy promotion, and strategic partnerships would ultimately be judged favorably—even where immediate outcomes proved painful or uncertain.

Whether that confidence proves warranted remains a subject of vigorous debate among historians, policymakers, and the American public.

---
